paras: The killing of Frank Gallup took place at Shenandoah, Iowa, on the night of August 11, 1888, when militiamen besieging his family's house shot dead a man accused of killing a merchant, F. J. Pine, and a crowd dragged his body through the streets on a rope. The first wire said a mob had hanged him to a tree, and the case circulated as a lynching before fuller dispatches described a militiaman's shot and the dragging of a corpse.

A day earlier a mob had twice taken Frank Phillips, a drayman jailed on a charge of attempting to assault Pine's six-year-old daughter, from the jail, tarring, feathering and whipping him and hoisting him up a telegraph pole until he confessed. A Wyoming paper's Shenandoah special called Phillips Gallup's friend, but an August 12 dispatch said reports of a connection were "not true."

On the evening of August 11 Frank and Charlie Gallup were reported to be beating their father when Pine and other neighbors went over to intervene, and Frank shot Pine through the heart without warning. Marshal Schwartz said he could not take Gallup without an armed force, so at Sheriff Skinner's call Captain Mount surrounded the house with twenty men of Company E, Fifth Regiment, while 100 to 500 armed citizens gathered.

Gallup's parents said he had fled, but as a search party left the cellar he appeared with two revolvers, shot the unarmed David Campbell in the neck, wounded T. H. Winfrey in the leg and killed militiaman Bert Rice. As he ran toward the rear of the house a young militiaman named Fletcher shot him at close range. When Gallup's wife said he was dead, the crowd, fearing a trick, made her fasten a rope around his neck, and "with wild cheers" dragged the naked body down the main street to the city hall, where hundreds viewed it.

Samuel Gallup and his wife were jailed and, after a crowd threatened them, taken to the county jail at Clarinda as accomplices. A coroner's inquest over Pine, Rice and Gallup reportedly brought out nothing differing from the published story. Gallup was buried "amidst the execrations of the inhabitants" in the potter's field, as popular feeling barred the family lot.

A Shenandoah dispatch commended the militia, Fletcher above all, and Campbell was expected to die, though no later report of his fate was found. No report of charges over Gallup's death or the dragging appears in the coverage. On September 25 the Omaha Bee reported that Samuel Gallup, "acquitted by the courts of complicity," had died of a stomach tumor.

The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined the first wire "Lynched at Midnight," and a Michigan paper ran it as "Lynchers at Work," its subhead confusing Gallop with the drayman of the Phillips case. Weekly digests kept that version, and the Worthington Advance in Minnesota used it to call Iowa "the banner state in the matter of lynching." The New York Evening World's brief had a ruffian who shot "nine men" lynched in Iowa.

From August 12 a fuller dispatch ran from Illinois to Maine under headlines such as "A Desperado's Death," and Nebraska, Kansas and Wyoming weeklies carried versions into late August. These accounts called Gallup a "desperado" and "brute" and praised his killers; the Wyoming paper said he had "met a just reward." Even so, an Omaha dispatch said he had been "strung up by frenzied citizens" before describing the rifle shot, and the Bee's year-end review said the crowd "dragged him to death." No account named anyone's race.

The first wire's mob hanging and the Bee's dragging to death conflict with the later, detailed and Iowa accounts, and with the inquest notice, all of which say Fletcher shot Gallup before the rope was applied. The shooting account is better supported because it came later, named those involved and was carried by Iowa papers.

reader.title: Killing of Frank Gallup
bases: Militia Company E, called out at the sheriff's request with armed citizens, besieged the house and a militiaman shot Gallup dead as he fired on them; the crowd then dragged his body with a rope (A13, A16, A3).

The detailed, later and Iowa accounts, and the inquest notice, say militiaman Fletcher shot Gallup during a lawful siege while Gallup was firing on the militia, and that only his corpse was roped and dragged (A13, A16, A17, A3); the first wire's mob hanging (A1, A2) and the Bee's 'dragged him to death' (A25) are contradicted by these fuller reports, so the killing does not meet the standard of an illegal killing by a group, though the crowd's treatment of the body was mob action.

Many reports agree that Gallup killed Pine and Rice and was himself killed at the house (A3, A4, A13, A16, A19, A23), but the first wire says a mob captured and hanged him (A1, A2, A18) and the Bee's review says he was dragged to death (A25).

accounts.label: First wire (Shenandoah, Aug. 11)
accounts.gist: Gallop killed Pine and two officers from an upper window and was captured by the mob and hanged to a tree at midnight.

accounts.label: Full Shenandoah wire (Aug. 12-13)
accounts.gist: Gallup shot Pine, then Campbell, Winfrey and Rice when the militia searched the house; militiaman Fletcher shot him through the body; his wife was made to rope the corpse, which was dragged through the streets.

accounts.label: Omaha dispatch (Times special and Aug. 13-14 versions)
accounts.gist: Same sequence with more detail (Patterson's search, mother's cartridges, naked body left on the city hall floor), adding the inquest and the old man's capture in a barn.

accounts.label: Iowa paper
accounts.gist: Audubon County Republican tells the family background, Pine's remark about another tarring and feathering, and the militia's call-out by the sheriff.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee year-end review
accounts.gist: Gallup was captured after killing two militiamen and wounding three, and the crowd dragged him to death with a rope around his neck.

framing.detail: First-day headlines 'Lynched at Midnight' and 'Lynchers at Work' reported a mob hanging without comment.
Accounts call Gallup a 'desperado', 'brute' and one of 'those mal-formed marplots upon humanity', and praise Fletcher's 'pluck'; one says he 'met a just reward'.
The Rock Island Argus headlined 'Mob Rule and Murder' and 'Iowa Citizens Set Aside the Law and Courts', aimed at the Phillips mob, while calling Gallup's death that of 'the murderer'.
The Worthington Advance used the reported lynching to call Iowa 'the banner state in the matter of lynching' with 'as full a quota of barbarians as any state'.

info: Saturday night, August 11, 1888, between about 9:30 and 10:30 p.m.
The Gallup house about 150 yards west of the C., B. & Q. depot, Shenandoah, Iowa
Frank Gallup (also printed Gallop), about thirty, shot dead by a militiaman; his body was then roped and dragged through the streets
Accused of shooting F. J. Pine, a hardware merchant, during a family quarrel, then killing militiaman Bert Rice and wounding David Campbell and T. H. Winfrey while resisting capture
Militia Company E, Fifth Regiment, Iowa National Guard under Capt. Mount, with armed citizens; militiaman Fletcher (Moroni/Marino/Morris/Manis/Mooney) fired the fatal shot; the crowd dragged the body
Samuel Gallup 'acquitted by the courts of complicity'; died September 25, 1888, of a stomach tumor
